title: Pronouns for clarity
keyIdea: Pronouns such as he, she, it and they stand in for a noun so you do not repeat it. Say the name first, then the pronoun points back to it, and it must match: one or many, a person or a thing. If a pronoun could mean two people, use a name or reword it. When someone does something to their own self, use a -self word such as myself or themselves.

kid: Sam packed Sam's bag. That sounds odd! We swap the second Sam for a short word: Sam packed his bag. Words like he, his, she, her, it and they are pronouns.
Say the name first. Then the pronoun points back to it. The pronoun must fit. Mia lost her hat. The dogs wagged their tails. The box fell, and it broke.
Watch out for muddles. Tom told Jack he was late. Who was late? We can't tell! Use a name to fix it: Tom told Jack, "I am late."
When you do something to you, add self. I made it myself. Ben hurt himself. They helped themselves. Hisself and theirselves are not right.
adult: At seven to nine, children learn to use pronouns to avoid repetition and to link sentences together. They also learn to spot when a pronoun is unclear. This is part of the Year 3 and 4 grammar programme. It covers personal pronouns (he, she, it, they), possessives (his, her, their, our) and reflexive pronouns (myself, himself, themselves).

The lab gives each skill its own action. Children tap repeated names to swap them, but must keep the first mention. They fill gaps while an arrow points back to the noun. They pick a clear rewrite when he could mean two people. They choose -self words that loop back to the doer. Then they find the muddled pronoun in short passages.

Common mistakes: replacing every name, including the first, so the reader never learns who he is; mismatching number, as in the dogs wagged its tails; leaving two possible people for one pronoun; and the non-standard forms hisself and theirselves. Another slip is using him or her where a -self word is needed, which changes the meaning.
To help, read your child's writing aloud and pause at each he, she or it. Ask: who is that? If there are two answers, add the name.

familyTip: When your child tells a story about two friends, stop at a he or she and ask, "Which one?" Then help them put the name back in so it is clear.

visual.caption: Is each sentence clear, or could the pronoun mean two things? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The cup fell, and it broke.
Ali saw Ben, and he ran.
Mum told Gran she was tired.
The boys met the men, and they won.
Amy and Zoe left. She cried.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: swap repeated names for pronouns, match pronouns to nouns, fix sentences where he could mean two people, and pick -self words.

practice.prompt: Which is the best way to write "Kim rode Kim's bike"?
practice.hint: Keep the name once, then use a pronoun for the repeat.
practice.explain: Kim rode her bike names Kim once and then her points back. She rode her bike never says who she is.

practice.prompt: The {n} ducks shook ___ wings. Which word fits?
practice.hint: Is it one duck or many ducks?
practice.explain: There are {n} ducks, more than one, so the pronoun is their: they shook their wings.

practice.prompt: "Lucy told Meg she had won." What is the problem?
choices: She could be Lucy or Meg
practice.hint: Ask: who had won? Could it be two people?
practice.explain: She could point to Lucy or to Meg, so we cannot tell who won. A name would fix it.

practice.hint: Jay did it to or for his own self. Which -self word is standard?
practice.explain: Jay painted all {n} pictures himself. Hisself is not standard, and him would mean someone else.

choices: Dan dropped his cup, and the cup broke.
Dan put the cup on the plate, and it broke.
He dropped it, and it broke.
pool.hint: Look for a pronoun that could mean two things, or one with no name to point to.
pool.explain: Saying the cup again makes it clear. In the second, it could be the cup or the plate. In the third, we never learn who he is.

pool.prompt: My {n} friends and I made the cake ___.
pool.hint: My friends and I means we. What is the -self word for we?
pool.explain: We did it, so use ourselves. That is true for all {n} friends and you together.

pool.prompt: "The cat chased the {n} mice until ___ hid." Which is clearest?
pool.hint: Who hid? A pronoun could point to the cat or the mice.
pool.explain: Saying the mice makes it clear that all {n} mice hid. It or he could be the cat.

pool.prompt: Which pronoun fits? "The tree lost ___ leaves."
pool.hint: A tree is one thing, not a person.
pool.explain: One thing that is not a person takes its: the tree lost its leaves. No apostrophe here.

pool.prompt: A child changes every Sam in a story to he, even the first one. What goes wrong?
choices: The reader never finds out who he is
pool.hint: A pronoun has to point back to a name.
pool.explain: A pronoun points back to a name. If Sam is never named, the reader cannot know who he is.

pool.prompt: "Nia saw ___ in the mirror." Nia is looking at her own face. Which word?
pool.hint: Nia sees her own self. Her alone would mean another girl.
pool.explain: Herself loops back to Nia. Her would mean she saw some other girl, and sheself is not a word.

pool.prompt: "Mum told Gran she was tired." It was Mum who was tired. Which is the clearest fix?
choices: Mum said to Gran, "I am tired."
She told her she was tired.
Mum told Gran she was very tired.
pool.hint: Make it plain who was tired. Could anyone still mix them up?
pool.explain: "I am tired" can only mean Mum, the speaker. More pronouns, or adding very, leave it muddled.
